purpose: Second pass on the same contour. The first pass (recorded below, merged) built the versioned scheme, kept legacy bcrypt verifying and added verifyPasswordWithUpgrade, and it deliberately left V6.2.8 at FAIL because a legacy account still truncated. It turns out the reason no legacy account was ever upgraded is simpler and worse than 'not yet universally in force': nothing called verifyPasswordWithUpgrade. Both login paths called verifyPassword, which cannot rewrite anything, so the control existed and was reachable from nowhere. This pass wires both login paths to the upgrading form, gives the rewrite a durable atomic write path under FORCE row level security, and re-decides the scrypt profile against the primary source rather than against the bcrypt cost already in use.

firstPass.outcome: merged; the scheme, the legacy verify and verifyPasswordWithUpgrade all landed and are unchanged here
firstPass.purpose: Implement a backward-compatible versioned password hashing scheme in source code, as the owner authorised, removing the silent truncation bcrypt applies at 72 bytes. Not a production deploy and not a bulk migration. New and changed passwords are written with scrypt from node:crypto; legacy bcrypt hashes keep verifying so no active user is locked out.

requiredInvariants: No database schema change. passwordHash is a plain string column, so changing the hash FORMAT touches no schema; this was checked rather than assumed, and it is what separates this item from V6.5.1 (#4682) where durable state would have required a column.
No new dependency. scrypt comes from node:crypto, so no licence, provenance, SBOM or vulnerability review is opened.

No invented cryptography. The scheme is scrypt with an explicit algorithm, version and parameter marker in the stored string; parsing fails closed on any unknown scheme, unknown version, non-numeric parameter, N that is not a power of two, malformed base64 or missing field.
Existing bcrypt hashes keep verifying. No active user is locked out, no forced reset, and no hash is ever rewritten without a password having been presented and verified.

The scrypt parameters were chosen by measuring against the bcrypt cost in use (338.8 ms versus 350.0 ms on the target stack), not from memory. Comparable work is mandatory here rather than cosmetic: DUMMY_PASSWORD_HASH stays bcrypt, and a cost divergence between the two login branches would reopen the timing oracle this module was written to close.

The existing timing-oracle suite is preserved, not weakened. One assertion that phrased the property as 'the same bcrypt rounds' is restated as the parameter pair it was measured against, because a stored password is no longer bcrypt; the intent is unchanged and still enforceable.

No wall-clock assertion is added to CI. The existing file explains that timing on shared runners is unstable and does not explain a failure; parameters are asserted instead, exactly as bcrypt's cost already is.
No production rollout, migration evidence or rollback plan is claimed. Production acceptance remains a separate, open item under separate authority.
apps/landing is not touched. No production, REG.RU, DNS, database or credential mutation.

Two existing specs asserted the stored hash was bcrypt and had to be restated, not deleted: password-hashing.spec.ts's equal-cost assertion, and gekta-registration.spec.ts's bcrypt.compare on the stored value. Both now assert the property that still matters - the stored value is a hash of that password, written under the measured-equivalent scheme - through the module's own verifier rather than a named algorithm. Every remaining bcrypt.getRounds assertion targets DUMMY_PASSWORD_HASH or comparisonHashFor(absent), which stay bcrypt by design and are untouched.

SUPERSEDED BY THIS PASS. The first pass recorded: "V6.2.8 deliberately stays FAIL. A legacy account still verifies through bcrypt and still truncates, so the requirement is not met for that population; claiming PASS on a working implementation that is not yet universally in force would be exactly the error this programme exists to avoid." That reasoning was right and its diagnosis was wrong. The implementation was not merely 'not yet universally in force' - it was in force nowhere, because neither login path called it. V6.2.8 moves to PASS on this pass, on the wiring and the write path, not on the scheme alone.
No bulk migration and no forced reset. A hash is rewritten only where the user has just proved the password, so the new format exists exactly where it was earned.

The order is fixed: verify against the stored hash first, and only on success compute the new one and write it conditionally. A failed rewrite never turns a correct password into a refusal - the password was already verified - and the next login tries again.
The rewrite is conditional on the exact previous hash. A concurrent password change or a parallel login that already upgraded wins, and this call reports that it changed nothing.

The write authority is dedicated, not borrowed. Owning the function by pc_password_reset_authority would have reused that role's policy and handed a format upgrade the full write rights of a password reset; pc_password_format_authority carries exactly one privilege, column-scoped to passwordHash.

public."users" is under FORCE row level security, so a SECURITY DEFINER function is still subject to the policies. Both policies are required: the UPDATE's WHERE clause reads passwordHash, and with only the UPDATE policy the statement matches no row. Found by running it on PostgreSQL 16, not by reading.

A format upgrade is not a credential change. credential_version is not bumped, password_changed_at is not written, no session is revoked and no notification is sent: revoking every session or raising a false security alert because the server re-encoded a password the user did not change would be worse than the truncation it fixes.

The scrypt profile is the one the primary source names, not one derived from the bcrypt cost already configured. This revises the first pass's basis: N=2^17 r=8 p=1 is the top rung OWASP publishes, and the earlier N=2^16 r=8 p=1 - chosen for equivalence with bcrypt cost 12 - appears nowhere on that ladder. Comparable work between the known and unknown login branches is unaffected: the branch lives inside verifyPassword and DUMMY_PASSWORD_HASH stays bcrypt.

The database schema does change on this pass, and the first pass's 'no database schema change' invariant is therefore scoped to it rather than to the contour. One nullable column is not added here; the migration adds a role, two policies and one SECURITY DEFINER function, and no column of public."users" is added or altered.
Applying the migration to production is a separate controlled exact-SHA release with its own authority. Merge is not deploy and CI is not a production proof.

The auth EXECUTE surface stays a closed enumeration, and this function joins it rather than routing around it. Migration 20260808180000 revokes ALL on schema auth from app_service and re-grants only a named list, so a function missing from that list is denied to the production runtime - which is what CI caught, and it caught it the hard way: a failed rewrite is deliberately swallowed so a bad write never turns a correct password into a refusal, so the denial did not break login, it just meant no hash was ever upgraded. The same shape of failure this whole pass exists to fix, one layer down. The function is now granted to app_service alongside the other auth principals, added to the registry the provisioning gate enforces, granted in the one-deal harness and the Kubernetes runtime grants, and revoked from every staff, storage, outbox and app principal exactly as replace_password_after_reset is.

A database dump carries the function but not the cluster-level role that owns it, so the DR rehearsal re-creates pc_password_format_authority, re-owns the function, restores the two column grants and re-applies the EXECUTE grant and revokes after restore - the same block every other authority already has. Without it a restored database has the function owned by whoever ran the restore, which is a definer with more rights than the authority was ever meant to carry.

The authority role is created with the full house flag set - NOLOGIN NOINHERIT NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE - and the migration raises if anything has been granted membership in it. The first version wrote only NOLOGIN and relied on defaults for the rest; NOINHERIT is the one that matters, because it is what stops a role granted membership from picking the rights up implicitly.

No path may assume the stored hash is bcrypt. organization-invitation.service.ts called bcrypt.compare directly in two places - the MFA recovery confirmation and the invitation-acceptance password proof - and both now go through verifyPassword. This was already broken before this pass: hashPassword has written scrypt since the versioned scheme landed, so an account whose password was set after that point already could not complete MFA recovery, and got MFA_RECOVERY_INVALID for a correct password. Upgrading legacy hashes on login made that universal rather than occasional, which is how a real acceptance run found it. V11.2.4's condition now forbids bcrypt comparison outside the owning module as well as bcrypt hashing.
acceptance: A password longer than 72 bytes is distinguished from one sharing its first 72 bytes, in ASCII and in Cyrillic, and the same pair is shown to collide under the old scheme so the change is demonstrated rather than asserted.
Legacy bcrypt hashes still verify, including the older $2a$ prefix.
Malformed, unknown-scheme and unknown-version records are refused and are never rehashed.
verifyPasswordWithUpgrade verifies before computing, passes the previous value as a precondition for a compare-and-set, and a failed write leaves the login valid and the old hash intact.
Restoring the truncating bcrypt scheme fails 8 of the 40 cases across both suites.
The matrix rebuilds at applied 332 / rejected 0 with no verdict moved: V6.2.8 remains FAIL with a rewritten, self-revoking condition naming what is left.
Both login paths call verifyPasswordWithUpgrade and pass a persist callback bound to upgradePasswordHashFormat; a test asserts the wiring rather than assuming it.

On live PostgreSQL 16: a legitimate upgrade returns true; a stale expected hash returns false; an unknown user returns false; the runtime roles cannot touch the table directly; the authority cannot write any other column and cannot delete.

Memory is bounded by measurement, not by preference. scrypt at 128 MiB runs on the libuv threadpool, four wide by default, so peak process RSS was 558 MiB at four concurrent verifications and 559 MiB at thirty-two: the burst becomes latency, not exhaustion. The ceiling is proportional to UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE, so 560 MiB is a measured ceiling on a four-core machine rather than a promise about a specific host.

V6.2.8 moves FAIL to PASS with seven self-revoking conditions. Eleven negative mutations each revoke the condition they target: the reverted profile, either login path returning to the non-upgrading verify, a dropped persist callback, a rewrite no longer conditional on the previous hash, a whole-table grant, a credential_version bump, a session revocation, a notification, and a removed legacy cost.

The omission check measures statements, not prose. Its first version asserted the absence of the words credential_version and password_changed_at and was revoked immediately by the comment that names both columns to say it does not write them; a comment-only mutation now leaves the decision standing while any of the five statements revokes it.
The matrix rebuilds at applied 332 / rejected 0, with FAIL falling from 102 to 101 and PASS rising to 118.

The provisioning gate passes with the new signature in AUTH_RUNTIME_FUNCTIONS, which means every source it checks grants it to the auth principal and revokes it from the staff principal - the gate fails if any one source is missed, which is the property that makes the enumeration worth having.

The persistent-auth acceptance suite passes 17/17 AND the database afterwards shows sixteen hashes no longer in bcrypt form. The count is the point: the suite passed just as cleanly while the upgrade was doing nothing at all, so a green suite alone never proved this control was in force.
